clips.title: How to Build a Slack App
clips.why: In two short chapters you see why an app must prove a request came from Slack, and how to answer Slack fast and do the slow work afterwards.
look: The signature check: Slack signs each request so a public URL cannot be faked. Our app has no public URL at all, because it uses Socket Mode.
The long-running task chapter: Slack will not wait for slow work, so the response goes back first and the work happens after.
However the video's app runs the slow work, the order is the point. In our app, the slow work after the answer is the Temporal signal.
clips.after: Our handlers follow the same order: ack() at once, then the signal to nova:RH-1234, then chat.update.

clips.title: A deep dive into Slack's Block Kit
clips.why: A short reminder that a Slack message with buttons is just JSON, which is why we can build Nova's plan message in code and test it.
look: A message that looks finished in Slack is written as plain JSON.
Notice that the message is a list of blocks, and each block has a type.
clips.after: Nova's plan message is the same kind of JSON: a section for the plan and an actions block with three buttons.

clips.title: A deep dive into Slack's Block Kit
clips.why: Here buttons and other interactive elements come alive: what Slack sends to your app when someone clicks.
look: Each interactive element has an action ID, and the click's payload names it, which is how the app knows which button was pressed.
Think about what the app must learn from a click: which button, who clicked, and in which message. Slack's click payload carries all three.
Later in the video (after this clip) his app receives clicks at a public URL. Socket Mode delivers the same payload over the WebSocket instead.
clips.after: Our Approve button's action_id is plan_approve and its value is nova:RH-1234|v2, so the click itself says which run and which plan version it decides.

practice.q: Put the Approve handler's steps in the right order.
items: Call ack(), so Slack knows the click arrived
Read the button's value to find the run and the plan version
Check that the person who clicked is the requester
Send the decidePlan signal with the person and the version
Edit the message with chat.update: who decided, no buttons
practice.why: ack() must come first because of the three-second limit. The check comes before the signal so a wrong click never reaches the run, and the edit comes last so the buttons disappear only once the decision was delivered.

practice.q: Finish the Approve button so that a click says which run and which plan version it decides.
practice.hint: The workflow ID, a vertical bar, then the plan version.
practice.why: The value is free text for the app's own use. With the workflow ID and the version in it, the handler can find the run, and an old button for v2 can never approve plan v3.

practice.q: Which Slack token opens the Socket Mode connection?

options.text: The app-level token, which starts with xapp- and has the connections:write scope
options.why: That token exists only to open the socket. The bot token is used for Web API calls like chat.postMessage.

options.text: The bot token, which starts with xoxb-
options.why: The bot token calls Slack's Web API. It cannot open the Socket Mode connection.

options.text: No token: Socket Mode is open to any app
options.why: Socket Mode needs an app-level token, so only our app can receive our app's events.

practice.q: Nova posts a question in RH-1234's thread. The app's message handler sees that post too. Which filter keeps it from counting as an answer?

options.why: Nova's question is inside the thread, so it has a thread_ts. This filter would let it through.

options.text: Skip messages that have a bot_id
options.why: Messages from bots carry a bot_id, Nova's included. Only people's replies become answerQuestion signals.

options.text: Skip messages longer than one line
options.why: People write long answers too. Length says nothing about who wrote it.
